transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (AtlasData CTO), Liam O'Connor (AtlasData Head of Platform), Renee Park (AtlasData ML Infra), Diego Marquez (Backend Eng), Anna Li (Product)

Auto-generated summary (may be rough): quick demo focusing on edge-cases - long context, high-TPS, streaming backpressure, timeouts; action items to run POC and share docs.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:05] Priya: yep, loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:08] Liam: morning all, exciting to see the edge-cases demo.
[00:12] Maya: cool! i'll keep this tight, samir will jump into the deep stuff. quick intro: redwood offers hosted, dedicated and private, and today we'll show some behavior under long-context and high throughput loads, plus streaming backpressure/timeouts.
[00:27] Samir: hi team. quick agenda: 1) long context window behavior + kv cache, 2) high TPS patterns and autoscale, 3) streaming and backpressure, 4) console + optimize recs, 5) q&a and next steps. sound good?
[00:36] Priya: yep. our main ask: we have 200k token docs per session and plan to run steady-state 800 qps for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). we need to know latency, cost, and stability.
[00:47] Jules: noted, 200k tokens is big; we usually shard context and use prefix caching. we'll demo how kv cache and chunking behaves.
[00:55] Renee: quick security baseline - we'll need SOC2, KMS, audit logs, and VPC peering for private deployment.
[01:02] Maya: yep we'll send the security pack; dedicated + VPC fits that.

[03:10] Samir: ok jumping into console - here's the request profile (shows fake link to dashboard). note per-route token breakdown, trace, and the chart showing sequence length distribution. when you have lots of long contexts we recommend model variants with kv-optimized kernels and chunked requests.
[03:35] Diego: when you say chunked requests, do you reassemble on the model side? latency implications?
[03:40] Samir: good q. we chunk on the client/ingest side, keep KV entries per chunk in the cache. on decode we stream tokens back and stitch at the app layer, latency per chunk can add ~10-40ms overhead depending on batch alignment. for 200k tokens you typically keep only the recent n chunks in kv to bound memory.
[04:08] Anna: will this break thread-safety across users if we shard?
[04:12] Jules: we partition by conversation id so it's isolated; cache keys have tenancy prefix. sometimes the transcript might mention "KV cash" in auto-notes but that's a typo.

[06:00] Samir: moving to high TPS - demo sim: start sustained 800 qps, bursts to 2k for 30s. we're running on Dedicated pool (simulated). watch the tracer: autoscaler adds nodes, batching increases, but we also show tail latency impact as sequence length varies.
[06:35] [system noise, someone speaks in background]
[06:42] Liam: can you show failure modes? what happens when backpressure occurs to streaming clients?
[06:47] Samir: yes. two modes: server-side backpressure where internal queues fill and we start shedding or falling back to cheaper model variants; and client-observed timeouts where a streaming connection stalls. we'll demo both.
[07:05] Samir: starting the load test now -> (noise) you'll see the streaming responses start then pause when the worker queue spikes.
[07:30] Priya: i'm seeing gaps in the stream, is that expected?
[07:34] Samir: expected during sustained oversubscription. Redwood supports partial-stream resume: we keep a per-request checkpoint so the client can reconnect and resume from last token, but this requires the client to reissue with the same request-id. sometimes transcription auto-labels that as a reconnect but it may be lost if client doesn't persist id.
[08:10] Diego: what about exactly-once vs at-least-once? we can't tolerate duplicates for certain analytics writes.
[08:18] Jules: streaming is at-least-once by default during reconnects; for dedupe you can use idempotency keys and sequence numbers. we also provide deterministic model shards for some models to reduce nondeterminism.

[10:00] Maya: quick interjection - i want to cover timeouts: client side typically sets 30s, 60s, etc. for very long-context decodes that can exceed client timeouts. we recommend client -> read timeout of at least 120s for some workflows and server-side early ack patterns for background completes.
[10:25] Priya: our front end has 45s socket timeouts, can we use background callbacks?
[10:29] Samir: yes, use async job mode: API accepts job, returns job id, and you poll or webhook for completion. that avoids streaming timeouts but adds complexity to UX.

[12:00] Samir: demo 2 - fallback policy: when Dedicated pool reaches threshold we show automatic fallback to hosted lower-cost model that has lower latency guarantees; you can tune the policy to prefer availability over quality or vice versa.
[12:22] Liam: how do we control routing by region? we need EU-only for some customers.
[12:28] Jules: routing policy has rules by tenant, region, and SLA; you can pin EU-only model variants + region. audit logs show every route decision.

[15:00] Samir: show optimize recommendations: batching windows, token-based batching, quantization profiles per model; for your RAG use-case we suggested int8 quantization on the 70b variant and a 40ms batching window to hit cost targets.
[15:25] Priya: any quality regressions from quant? we can't drop below a certain rouge/bleu threshold.
[15:31] Samir: Optimize includes evaluation harness - you can run your prompts through both quantized and full-precision and get per-prompt deltas; threshold alerts can block rollouts.

[18:00] Priya: back to streaming: what about TCP connection limits, nginx timeouts at our edge?
[18:08] Maya: good ops detail. if you have edge timeouts, webhook/callback or async job mode circumvents it. also recommend long-lived multiplexed connections and a retry policy with exponential backoff.

[20:00] Diego: curious about KV cache evictions: if we evict mid-generation, what happens?
[20:06] Samir: if a KV entry is missing we recompute the prefix for that chunk which adds latency; we try to proactively warm cache for expected prefixes. we also show cache hit/miss charts.

[22:30] Samir: showing console traces - per-token breakdown, queue depth heatmap, and a streaming timeline. note the callout where we saw timeouts during the 2k burst - that was the backpressure window.
[23:00] Liam: can we enforce hard concurrency limits per-tenant? we want to avoid noisy neighbors.
[23:05] Jules: yes, per-tenant QPS caps and per-route concurrency; avalanching protections can reject requests with graceful 429s and give retry-after headers.

[25:10] Priya: SLA questions - what uptime and latency SLAs do you offer for dedicated?
[25:15] Maya: dedicated has a 99.9% uptime SLA up to the committed throughput; latency SLOs are discussed per model/shape in the performance profile. we'll include the SLA matrix in the pricing pack.

[28:00] Samir: demo of reconnect/resume: i force-terminate a streaming connection (simulating edge disconnect) and reconnect with same request-id. watch tokens resume around the last checkpoint.
[28:22] Anna: nice. any caveats for ordering or token gaps?
[28:28] Samir: there can be small overlap; clients should dedupe by sequence number. we try to avoid re-sending too many tokens by recording last-acked offset.

[31:00] Renee: security follow-ups - can you support customer-managed keys (HSM)?
[31:05] Maya: yes, KMS and HSM integrations are supported for private/dedicated; we'll attach the KMS note. also audit logs available for all requests.

[33:30] Samir: performance tuning tips: 1) tune batch window based on your latency/throughput tradeoff, 2) pre-warm caches for long-context sessions, 3) use quantized variants for cost but run evals first, 4) use per-route concurrency caps and fallback policies.

[36:00] Liam: about the POC - we need a script that simulates our RAG flow, 200k tokens into context and 800 qps sustained. Also need a cost estimate for Dedicated vs hosted for 1-week run.
[36:12] Maya: Samir will deliver the script and a sample pricing estimate. we can provision a short-lived dedicated pool for the POC or run in hosted with priority.

[38:40] Diego: any runtime logs we can grab for debugging? we prefer structured traces.
[38:45] Jules: console supports traces + downloadable HAR-like streaming logs with token-level timestamps; we also push to your logging sink via our log forwarder.

[41:00] Priya: what's the path for on-prem/private - our compliance folks ask for air-gapped options.
[41:06] Maya: private deployment can be air-gapped; it's a separate engagement, requires an on-prem agent and offline package. support and upgrades are via secure channels. we'll include higher-level notes.

[43:00] Maya: ok recap and next steps. who owns the POC on your side?
[43:06] Liam: i'll own infra, Priya will own success criteria, Renee will handle security checks.
[43:11] Maya: perfect. next steps: we'll send pricing + SLA + security docs, Samir will share benchmark script, we'll schedule POC between Dec 15-22 pending your dataset.
[43:25] Priya: sounds good. one ask: can you include a recommended nginx timeout and client retry policy in the doc?
[43:30] Maya: yes will add.

[46:00] Maya: any final q's?
[46:05] Diego: not for me.
[46:07] Anna: none.
[46:09] Priya: thank you all, this was useful.
[46:12] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

End of meeting.
